messages.author: 7d7bd1f061fa8249
messages.subject: Several initial questions from a Lavaan newbie.
parts:
1.   I just ran my first try at estimating a correlation matrix for my first Lavaan efa, using polychoric correlation.  17 variables, the first 14 defined as "ordered," and the final three as "numeric":
cor2 <- lavCor(csbx1, missing = 'pairwise', output = 'cor')
I got a perfectly good looking correlation matrix, but with the warning message:
Warning message:
In lavaan(slotParTable = PT.un, slotData = lav.data, model.type = "unrestricted",  :
  lavaan WARNING: estimation of the baseline model failed.
I was a little surprised, because I don't think that I hypothesized any model.  I recognize that this is a warning and not an error.  But I am concerned that there may be something off kilter with my call or my data.  Does this warning suggest that there is something that I should check about it before continuing?

2.  Another warning as I run my first Lavaan efa.  I suspect that this warning is related to the fact that there is some missing data, so that the call had to use the "missing = 'pairwise' parameter.  Am I supposed to do some "smoothing" now to get rid of the (impossible) negative variances?  And how to I output the cor/cov tables?
> efa1 <- efaUnrotate(csbx1, nf=4, missing = 'pairwise')
Warning message:
In lav_object_post_check(object) :
  lavaan WARNING: some estimated ov variances are negative
3.  I don't know how to look at the variances here.  So I did an oblique rotation:
> efa2 <- oblqRotate(efa1, method = 'quartimin')
> efa2

Hi Lawrence
in my experience this type of result for factor 3

ct                       1.015*        
ci               0.159*  0.945*

suggests that the 2 items are highly redundant--the correlation between them is likely to be high. If so this might be in Cattell's words a 'bloated specific'. I explore this by removing one of those items and rerunning the EFA. That usually removes one factor and moves the retained variable to a sensible location. 
see: Cattell, R. B., & Tsujioka, B. (1964). The Importance of Factor-Trueness and Validity, Versus Homogeneity and Orthogonality, in Test Scales. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 24(1), 3-30.

messages.subject: Re: Several initial questions from a Lavaan newbie.
parts:
can you show str(csbx1), to see what you feeding into the efa function? You said you have both categorical and cintinuous variables, this can be handled by the fundtion, but need to specify the right type for each variable

Why did you pick the 4 factor solution? You are going to want to test EFA for 1,2,3,4,5 ... number of factors and based on fit indices decide how many factors should be extracted. What I recommend is to look at 2 or 3 number of factors that have good model fit, and then decide between them in function of theoretical interpretation based on the factor loadings and factor correlations.

The best fit indices, in the sense that are less affected by other model/data characteristics would be CFI and gamma-hat, also can look at information criteria such as AIC and BIC

the efa object is a lavaan object so you can get the fit indices as
fitMeasures(efa1)
moreFitindices(efa1)

Thanks, Mauricio:  
Here's my data frame.
'data.frame':	460 obs. of  18 variables:
 $ g       : Ord.factor w/ 4 levels "0"<"1"<"2"<"3": 2 1 1 1 3 1 1 1 4 1 ...
 $ t       : Ord.factor w/ 4 levels "0"<"1"<"2"<"3": 2 1 1 1 1 1 3 3 2 1 ...

 $ cv      : Ord.factor w/ 4 levels "0"<"1"<"2"<"3": 2 2 1 2 2 2 1 3 4 2 ...
 $ ah      : Ord.factor w/ 4 levels "0"<"1"<"2"<"3": 3 2 2 2 3 3 2 2 4 1 ...
 $ tatr    : Ord.factor w/ 4 levels "0"<"1"<"2"<"3": 3 2 1 2 3 2 3 1 3 1 ...
 $ iatr    : Ord.factor w/ 4 levels "0"<"1"<"2"<"3": 3 1 1 1 4 1 3 3 3 1 ...

 $ c4glom  : Ord.factor w/ 6 levels "1"<"2"<"3"<"4"<..: 2 1 2 2 2 2 1 2 2 2 ...

 $ maxdsa1 : num  0.209 -0.31 0.209 -0.31 NA ...
 $ maxdsa2 : num  -0.536 -0.536 0.273 -0.536 NA ...
 $ gfr_biop: num  0.475 3.042 0.377 2.536 0.685 ...

I chose four factors because that was what was suggested by fa.parallel.  But I now realize that adding a fifth factor might be a good idea.  When I ran a five factor model, the original four factors were still clearly evident and interpretable, and the fifth factor turned out also to be clearly interpretable, important, and quite distinct from each of the first four.  I'll try the various fit measures that you have suggested.  
On another line, I thought that the warnings dealing with non-positive definite matrices might be due to missing data.  But there really isn't much 80% of the cases are complete, and only 2% of the actual data points are missing.  Gavin (above) suggested that the problem might be entering into the data matrix variables that are too highly correlated (leading to near singluarity, I expect).  I'll try deleting a couple of variables that are almost perfectly correlated to see if that gets rid of some of the warnings.  I really wish I understood better what all the warnings mean and how worrisome they may be.  One warning was that 
"46 cells were adjusted for 0 values..."  If this refers to the 4^14 =  268435456 cells in the cross-tabulation of the factor variables, it doesn't seem to serious to me.  But these warnings are so cryptic to a newby like me, and I can't find anywhere that they are explained.
Thanks for your help. Larry

messages.subject: Re: Several initial questions from a Lavaan newbie.
parts: I can't find a function testLoadings(), and I don't know how to correct the standard error for the variance of the rotation function.  Is this something that I need to deal with?

The full warning is simply telling you not to trust the significance tests of the rotated solution.  It was a very ad hoc approach to EFA using lavaan that Sunthud wrote years ago, and development did not proceed very far.  You can still make decisions using the standardized loadings based on their magnitude, rather than testing them for statistical significance.  It is exploratory, so you shouldn't proceed as though you have a priori null hypotheses to test anyway.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
